title: The merging galaxy pair NGC 4568 and NGC 4567
caption: The interacting galaxies NGC 4568 and NGC 4567, imaged by the Gemini North telescope
credit: International Gemini Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA. Image processing: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), J. Miller (Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab), M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) & D. de Martin (NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: Official NSF NOIRLab / Gemini press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: Two spiral galaxies, NGC 4568 at the bottom and NGC 4567 at the top, appear together in this view from the Gemini North telescope in Hawai‘i. The pair are interacting, just beginning to clash and merge, in the direction of the constellation Virgo.

In around 500 million years, the two are expected to have become a single elliptical galaxy. Mergers like this can transform galaxies completely. The orderly disks and spiral arms are scrambled by gravity, and the stars settle into a smoother, rounder system. Gas pushed together during the collision can also spark bursts of new star formation along the way.

The object list also includes SN 2020fqv. The SN prefix marks a supernova, or exploding star. The picture was taken through g, r, i and hydrogen-alpha filters, the last of which picks out the red glow of hydrogen gas in regions where stars are forming.

understand.summary: Taken in visible light with the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph on Gemini North through g, r, i and hydrogen-alpha filters. The color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The long exposure gathers far more light than the eye.
